screens.title: Why planning matters for database projects
screens.narratorSegment: Planning is not paperwork — it is the activity that shapes how a database will deliver value. In practice, planning collects what stakeholders need, decides which requirements are in scope, and defines measurable acceptance criteria so developers and testers know when a feature is complete. For example, if marketing wants a customer activity report, planning clarifies which fields the report must include, which users can view it, and what response-time is acceptable. A common misconception is that planning delays delivery. In reality, shallow planning creates hidden assumptions that lead to rework and delays. Another pitfall is analysis paralysis: spending excessive time seeking perfect requirements. The practical balance is to gather a minimum viable set of requirements, implement a small slice, get feedback, and iterate. This reduces risk by validating assumptions early. Remember that planning should capture both what the system must do and how well it must perform. The core insight: thoughtful planning converts vague needs into concrete, testable work so the team builds the right database features. Why planning matters for database projects means capture measurable acceptance criteria and iterate quickly to validate assumptions and reduce risk.. In practical terms, define success before you design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Why planning matters
Definition

Planning shapes outcomes, not paperwork.

Good planning turns stakeholder needs into clear, testable requirements and measurable success criteria.

Explanation
  • Collect stakeholder needs and translate them into actionable items.
  • Define acceptance criteria with measurable metrics so features can be validated.
  • Prevent hidden assumptions that cause rework through early validation cycles.
Concrete example
If a report is needed, specify fields, filters, user roles and a maximum query time so indexing and caching decisions are clear.
Key Takeaway

Plan to define success and validate assumptions early; this reduces rework and delivers real value faster.

Common mistakes
  • Jumping to design before requirements are validated.
  • Over-documenting to the point of delay without a feedback plan.
  • Not setting measurable non-functional targets, making acceptance subjective.
Pro tip

Capture a minimal viable requirement set, implement one slice, and gather feedback to refine the rest.

screens.title: Identifying stakeholders and their roles
screens.narratorSegment: Stakeholders are anyone who has an interest in or is affected by the database. Identifying them is essential because each group highlights different requirements and constraints. Typical stakeholder groups include end-users, who care about usability and the exact data they need to complete tasks; business analysts, who care about reports, data integrity and traceability; system administrators and DBAs, who focus on performance, backups, and operability; product managers and project managers, who prioritize scope and timelines; and legal or compliance teams, who impose constraints around data privacy and retention. When you list stakeholders, add a short description of their primary interest to avoid assumptions. A common mistake is to consult only the loudest or most accessible stakeholders; this biases requirements. Another pitfall is treating stakeholders as a single monolithic group instead of recognizing internal differences. For example, power users and casual users often have different needs. The practical action is to create a stakeholder map, rank influence and interest, and plan targeted activities to gather each group's inputs. Who are the three stakeholders you must talk to first for your next project?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Stakeholders
Stakeholder Hierarchy
End-users
Need clear data access and usable queries for their tasks.
Business analysts / Product

Admins / DBAs
Need operational metrics, backups, and maintainability support.
Legal / Compliance

Avoid this bias

Do not only interview the most available person. Seek a balanced set of perspectives to avoid missing hidden constraints.

Practical technique: influence vs interest map
  1. List stakeholder groups and key representatives.
  2. Score each for influence and interest to prioritize outreach.
  3. Plan tailored elicitation activities for high-influence or high-interest groups.
Concrete scenario
For an event system, talk to event planners, customer support, and finance for different requirements: scheduling, attendee experience, and billing data.
Key Takeaway

Identify and prioritize stakeholders early so you capture all requirements and prevent surprises later.

screens.title: Techniques for gathering requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Gathering requirements uses multiple techniques because different approaches reveal different kinds of information. Interviews give depth: a one-on-one conversation lets you probe motivations and constraints. Workshops create shared understanding by bringing several stakeholders together to negotiate trade-offs and priorities. Surveys scale breadth: they quantify preferences across a larger population but need carefully designed questions. Observing existing processes uncovers tacit knowledge that stakeholders may not verbalize, such as manual steps or hidden workarounds. When you plan elicitation, choose techniques intentionally. For a small project, a few focused interviews plus observation can be enough. For system-wide changes, combine workshops with surveys and follow-ups. Document everything — meeting notes, agreed decisions, and open questions — and record action items. A typical mistake is not validating captured requirements back with stakeholders. After initial capture, share concise summaries for confirmation to prevent misunderstandings. Which technique will reveal the most about how users really work? In practical terms, interviews, workshops, surveys and observation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Gathering Techniques
Techniques
Interviews
Deep, contextual, and best for understanding motivations and constraints.
Workshops
Good for aligning multiple stakeholders and negotiating scope.
Surveys
Quantifies preferences at scale; design questions carefully to be actionable.
Observation
Reveals tacit practices, workarounds and environmental constraints.
Documenting results
Record notes, decisions, open questions and action items. Validate summaries back with stakeholders to confirm intent.
Example plan
  1. Interview product owner and two power users.
  2. Observe event registration flow for one week.
  3. Run a workshop to align on reporting needs.
  4. Follow up with a short survey to 50 casual users.
Common mistake

Collecting raw notes without synthesizing them into user stories or acceptance criteria leaves developers guessing. Always convert findings into testable requirements.

Key Takeaway

Choose techniques that fit the problem size and validate captured requirements to avoid misinterpretation.

screens.title: Functional requirements for a database
screens.narratorSegment: Functional requirements describe the behavior and capabilities the system must provide. For a database project this typically includes the data entities to store, the queries and filters users must run, business rules for data changes, and permissions for who may read or update which data. Express these requirements as user stories or use cases; they should be concrete and tied to user goals. For example: 'As an event organizer, I want to view registrants for an event so that I can manage attendance.' That story implies entities like event, attendee, and registration, fields to store, and the ability to query by event ID. A common misconception is that functional requirements are the same as technical design. They are not: functional requirements say what must happen, not how you will implement it. Keep them implementation-agnostic so architects can propose the best design given non-functional constraints. When you write functional requirements, include acceptance criteria that clarify success and enable testing. Functional requirements for a database means functional requirements state user goals and expected behaviors; keep them implementation-agnostic and testable.. In practical terms, what the system must do — stored data, queries, and rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Functional Requirements
What they describe
  • Data entities and fields to store.
  • Operations users must perform: queries, writes, updates.
  • Business rules and permissions for data changes.
User story example
As an event organizer, I want to view registrants for an event so that I can manage attendance. Acceptance: list shows name, ticket type, and check-in status; query returns within 2s for up to 10,000 records.
Common pitfalls
Writing technical implementation details instead of user-focused behaviors.
Missing acceptance criteria that make requirements testable.
How to write better
  1. Use user stories describing role, action, and benefit.
  2. Add acceptance criteria that are measurable and verifiable.
  3. Keep stories independent and implementation-agnostic.
Key Takeaway

Write functional requirements as user-focused stories with acceptance criteria so engineers can deliver the behavior you expect.

screens.title: Non-functional requirements and measurable metrics
screens.narratorSegment: Non-functional requirements define constraints and qualities: how the system should behave rather than what it does. Typical categories include performance (response times), scalability (concurrent users or data volume), security (encryption, access controls), availability (uptime targets), and maintainability (ease of schema changes). These requirements often drive architecture decisions: a two-second query target may require indexing, caching or denormalization, while a 99.9% uptime target influences replication and failover choices. A frequent mistake is to leave non-functional requirements vague. Instead, define measurable metrics and acceptance criteria, for example: 'Event search queries must return results within 500 milliseconds for common filters under 1,000 concurrent users.' Another misconception is to treat non-functional requirements as secondary; they are central because they constrain feasible designs. Work with stakeholders to select which non-functional metrics matter for the system, and include them in the requirements so architects can design to meet them. Non-functional requirements and measurable metrics means make non-functional requirements measurable so they directly inform architecture and tests.. In practical terms, how the system must perform and operate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Non-functional Requirements
Categories & examples
Performance
Queries return within a time budget, e.g. 500 ms.
Scalability
Support N concurrent users or M rows without degradation.
Security
Encryption at rest and in transit; access controls.
Availability
Uptime target, e.g. 99.9%.
Concrete metric
All event registration queries must complete within 500 milliseconds under 1,000 concurrent users.
Why measurable metrics matter
  • They let architects choose appropriate designs and justify trade-offs.
  • They provide clear acceptance criteria for testing and operations.
  • They prevent vague promises that fail in production.
Common misconception

Treating non-functional requirements as optional or unspecified makes them impossible to validate and often leads to systems that are slow, insecure, or hard to maintain.

Key Takeaway

Define non-functional requirements with measurable targets so architecture and acceptance testing can be aligned to business expectations.

screens.title: From stakeholder conversation to user story
screens.narratorSegment: A user story is the bridge between stakeholder conversations and engineering work. Start by collecting raw inputs: notes from interviews, observed steps, and workshop outcomes. Synthesize these into a short role-based story: 'As a [role], I want [action] so that [benefit].' Add acceptance criteria that specify what success looks like, including any non-functional targets. For instance, from an organizer saying they need to check in attendees quickly, write: 'As an event attendant, I want to check in a guest by ticket ID so that entry is faster.' Acceptance: check-in completes within 250ms for offline cached lookups; only staff with the role 'event staff' can mark check-ins. A common mistake is writing stories that are too broad. If a story contains multiple unrelated actions, break it into smaller stories. Smaller stories are easier to estimate, implement, and test. Use the story as the basis for schema decisions and for creating tests that validate acceptance criteria. This keeps work focused and measurable. In practical terms, turn interviews and observations into actionable stories. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › User Stories
Make a story

Collect inputs, synthesize a short role-action-benefit sentence, and add measurable acceptance criteria.

Example
As an event organizer, I want to view registrants for an event so that I can manage attendance. Acceptance: shows name, ticket type, check-in status; queries must return within 2s for 10,000 records.
Split large stories

If a story bundles multiple features, split it so each piece can be completed and validated independently.

From story to schema
  1. Identify entities implied by the story (event, attendee, registration).

screens.title: Requirements influence architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Requirements drive architecture. When you have a clear set of functional and non-functional requirements, architects can choose a database design that meets them. For instance, frequent complex joins for reporting may lead to a normalized OLTP schema plus a separate analytics store. Tight response-time targets might require indexes, read replicas, or caching. High availability and compliance needs may push you toward multi-region replication and auditing mechanisms. The misconception is that architecture is a purely technical decision; in reality it balances business priorities, budget, and measurable constraints from requirements. Architects should consult the traceability of requirements to see which features and metrics are highest priority, and then document trade-offs. This keeps the architecture grounded in the needs it must satisfy. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Architecture Impact
Map requirements to patterns
Performance target → Indexing / Caching
If response time is strict, prioritize index design and caching strategies.
High concurrency → Read replicas / Partitioning
Scale reads with replicas and partition heavy tables for throughput.
Reporting needs → Separate analytics store
Avoid mixing OLTP and heavy analytic queries by offloading reports.
Trade-offs and risks

Every architectural choice introduces trade-offs: caching improves latency but adds consistency complexity; denormalization speeds reads but increases update complexity. Document these trade-offs tied to requirements so stakeholders understand impacts on cost and maintenance.

Concrete action
List top requirements, map each to candidate patterns, and note the risks and estimated cost for each option before deciding.
Key Takeaway

Let requirements drive architectural choices and document trade-offs so decisions are transparent and traceable to business needs.

screens.title: Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)
screens.narratorSegment: A Requirements Traceability Matrix is a structured document that links each requirement to its supporting design, implementation tasks, and validation tests. The purpose is to ensure nothing is lost from the initial stakeholder conversation to the final testing and deployment. An RTM typically lists requirement IDs, requirement descriptions, the related user story or use case, the design artifacts (ER diagrams, schema changes), development tickets, and test cases that verify acceptance criteria. For example, a registration requirement would reference the registration table schema, the A P I endpoint implementation ticket, and the automated test that asserts response time and data integrity under a given load. A common mistake is letting the RTM become stale. Treat it as a living artifact and update it as design and scope evolve. The RTM helps you demonstrate coverage during testing and makes change impact analysis much easier when new requests arrive. Design: registration table, index on event_id, view registrant_list

screens.title: Common pitfalls: scope creep and analysis paralysis
screens.narratorSegment: Two common planning risks pull projects in opposite directions. Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion of requirements without adjusting schedule or resources; it usually happens when change requests are accepted informally. The right response is to document new requests, assess impact on time and costs, and discuss trade-offs with stakeholders before committing. Analysis paralysis happens when teams over-collect without delivering, seeking perfect requirements before shipping anything. The opposite cure is to adopt an iterative approach: capture a minimum viable set of requirements, deliver a small slice, gather feedback, and refine. Both risks hurt delivery, so balance is essential. Use change control for formal requests and a short feedback loop for validation. A practical tool is to record each request and its impact in the RTM and require stakeholder sign-off for scope changes that materially affect schedule or cost. Which risk is more likely in your organization, and how will you prevent it? content.html:

Scope creep

Uncontrolled feature additions without adjusting time or resources leads to delays and quality problems.

How to manage
  • Document every change request and assess impact.
  • Discuss trade-offs with stakeholders and require sign-off for major scope changes.
  • Update RTM and timelines when scope changes are approved.
Analysis paralysis

Excessive planning without delivering prevents feedback and slows progress.

How to manage

  • Deliver small increments and collect real user feedback.
  • Refine requirements based on observed behavior rather than assumptions.

Balance careful capture with short delivery cycles; use impact assessment to manage requested changes.

fullNarratorScript:
When you begin a database project, the most important work happens before any tables are created. In this lesson you will learn how careful planning and clear requirements reduce rework, prevent surprises, and make your database deliver useful, maintainable results. We will walk through who to talk to, how to capture what they need, and how to turn those needs into functional tasks and measurable acceptance criteria. You will see concrete examples of functional and non-functional requirements, and how a simple user story can guide schema choices. We will also highlight common pitfalls, like starting implementation too early or letting scope grow without governance, and we will show practical ways to keep planning iterative so the system evolves with real feedback. By the end you will be able to list stakeholders, write clear user stories for a feature, and propose the non-functional metrics that matter for performance, security and scalability. Think of this as the blueprint phase: good planning makes construction faster and safer. What problem will your next database solve, and who must agree on the answer?

By the end of this chapter you will identify the right stakeholders, distinguish functional from non-functional requirements, and translate business needs into actionable specifications. You will be able to apply techniques like interviews and workshops to gather requirements, and you will document those findings so they support design and testing. This chapter also teaches how to set measurable non-functional criteria — for example, response-time targets or availability percentages — and why those metrics matter for operational success. Finally, you will learn to work iteratively: gather initial requirements, implement a small slice, collect feedback, and refine the plan. These skills let you reduce rework, avoid scope creep, and ensure the database delivers real value to users. Learning Objectives means translate stakeholder needs into testable requirements so every feature links back to business value.. In practical terms, what you will be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These objectives focus on the practical techniques you will use on real projects. You will practice stakeholder interviews and workshops so you can elicit both explicit and tacit requirements. You will translate requirements into user stories and acceptance criteria that developers and testers can act on. You will also learn to write non-functional requirements with measurable metrics, and to explain why those metrics matter — for example, how a two-second query target affects indexing and caching decisions. Finally, you will practice documenting requirements in a traceability matrix so you can show where each feature came from and how it will be validated. These are hands-on skills that reduce ambiguity and help teams deliver stable, useful databases. Learning Objectives — Skills and Practices means turn interviews and workshops into user stories and measurable acceptance criteria to guide design and testing.. In practical terms, practical abilities you'll practice and demonstrate. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Planning is not paperwork — it is the activity that shapes how a database will deliver value. In practice, planning collects what stakeholders need, decides which requirements are in scope, and defines measurable acceptance criteria so developers and testers know when a feature is complete. For example, if marketing wants a customer activity report, planning clarifies which fields the report must include, which users can view it, and what response-time is acceptable. A common misconception is that planning delays delivery. In reality, shallow planning creates hidden assumptions that lead to rework and delays. Another pitfall is analysis paralysis: spending excessive time seeking perfect requirements. The practical balance is to gather a minimum viable set of requirements, implement a small slice, get feedback, and iterate. This reduces risk by validating assumptions early. Remember that planning should capture both what the system must do and how well it must perform. The core insight: thoughtful planning converts vague needs into concrete, testable work so the team builds the right database features. Why planning matters for database projects means capture measurable acceptance criteria and iterate quickly to validate assumptions and reduce risk.. In practical terms, define success before you design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Stakeholders are anyone who has an interest in or is affected by the database. Identifying them is essential because each group highlights different requirements and constraints. Typical stakeholder groups include end-users, who care about usability and the exact data they need to complete tasks; business analysts, who care about reports, data integrity and traceability; system administrators and DBAs, who focus on performance, backups, and operability; product managers and project managers, who prioritize scope and timelines; and legal or compliance teams, who impose constraints around data privacy and retention. When you list stakeholders, add a short description of their primary interest to avoid assumptions. A common mistake is to consult only the loudest or most accessible stakeholders; this biases requirements. Another pitfall is treating stakeholders as a single monolithic group instead of recognizing internal differences. For example, power users and casual users often have different needs. The practical action is to create a stakeholder map, rank influence and interest, and plan targeted activities to gather each group's inputs. Who are the three stakeholders you must talk to first for your next project?

Gathering requirements uses multiple techniques because different approaches reveal different kinds of information. Interviews give depth: a one-on-one conversation lets you probe motivations and constraints. Workshops create shared understanding by bringing several stakeholders together to negotiate trade-offs and priorities. Surveys scale breadth: they quantify preferences across a larger population but need carefully designed questions. Observing existing processes uncovers tacit knowledge that stakeholders may not verbalize, such as manual steps or hidden workarounds. When you plan elicitation, choose techniques intentionally. For a small project, a few focused interviews plus observation can be enough. For system-wide changes, combine workshops with surveys and follow-ups. Document everything — meeting notes, agreed decisions, and open questions — and record action items. A typical mistake is not validating captured requirements back with stakeholders. After initial capture, share concise summaries for confirmation to prevent misunderstandings. Which technique will reveal the most about how users really work? Techniques for gathering requirements means combine interviews, workshops, surveys and observation to capture both explicit and tacit requirements.. In practical terms, interviews, workshops, surveys and observation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Functional requirements describe the behavior and capabilities the system must provide. For a database project this typically includes the data entities to store, the queries and filters users must run, business rules for data changes, and permissions for who may read or update which data. Express these requirements as user stories or use cases; they should be concrete and tied to user goals. For example: 'As an event organizer, I want to view registrants for an event so that I can manage attendance.' That story implies entities like event, attendee, and registration, fields to store, and the ability to query by event ID. A common misconception is that functional requirements are the same as technical design. They are not: functional requirements say what must happen, not how you will implement it. Keep them implementation-agnostic so architects can propose the best design given non-functional constraints. When you write functional requirements, include acceptance criteria that clarify success and enable testing. Functional requirements for a database means functional requirements state user goals and expected behaviors; keep them implementation-agnostic and testable.. In practical terms, what the system must do — stored data, queries, and rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Non-functional requirements define constraints and qualities: how the system should behave rather than what it does. Typical categories include performance (response times), scalability (concurrent users or data volume), security (encryption, access controls), availability (uptime targets), and maintainability (ease of schema changes). These requirements often drive architecture decisions: a two-second query target may require indexing, caching or denormalization, while a 99.9% uptime target influences replication and failover choices. A frequent mistake is to leave non-functional requirements vague. A user story is the bridge between stakeholder conversations and engineering work. Start by collecting raw inputs: notes from interviews, observed steps, and workshop outcomes. Synthesize these into a short role-based story: 'As a [role], I want [action] so that [benefit].' Add acceptance criteria that specify what success looks like, including any non-functional targets. For instance, from an organizer saying they need to check in attendees quickly, write: 'As an event attendant, I want to check in a guest by ticket ID so that entry is faster.' Requirements drive architecture. When you have a clear set of functional and non-functional requirements, architects can choose a database design that meets them. For instance, frequent complex joins for reporting may lead to a normalized OLTP schema plus a separate analytics store. Tight response-time targets might require indexes, read replicas, or caching. High availability and compliance needs may push you toward multi-region replication and auditing mechanisms. A Requirements Traceability Matrix is a structured document that links each requirement to its supporting design, implementation tasks, and validation tests. The purpose is to ensure nothing is lost from the initial stakeholder conversation to the final testing and deployment. An RTM typically lists requirement IDs, requirement descriptions, the related user story or use case, the design artifacts (ER diagrams, schema changes), development tickets, and test cases that verify acceptance criteria. For example, a registration requirement would reference the registration table schema, the A P I endpoint implementation ticket, and the automated test that asserts response time and data integrity under a given load. A common mistake is letting the RTM become stale. Treat it as a living artifact and update it as design and scope evolve. Two common planning risks pull projects in opposite directions. Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion of requirements without adjusting schedule or resources; it usually happens when change requests are accepted informally. The right response is to document new requests, assess impact on time and costs, and discuss trade-offs with stakeholders before committing. Analysis paralysis happens when teams over-collect without delivering, seeking perfect requirements before shipping anything. The opposite cure is to adopt an iterative approach: capture a minimum viable set of requirements, deliver a small slice, gather feedback, and refine. Both risks hurt delivery, so balance is essential. Use change control for formal requests and a short feedback loop for validation. A practical tool is to record each request and its impact in the RTM and require stakeholder sign-off for scope changes that materially affect schedule or cost. Before moving to design and implementation, run a short readiness checklist to reduce surprises. Confirm you have identified key stakeholders and validated summaries with them. Ensure functional requirements are written as user stories with acceptance criteria, and that non-functional requirements include measurable metrics with realistic targets. Keep these core concepts top of mind as you plan database work. Stakeholders are people or groups who care about or are affected by the project; map them and prioritize whose input matters most. Use cases and user stories connect actions to user benefits and guide schema and A P I design. Remember: write requirements so they are testable and avoid mixing implementation details into requirements.
